title: Vand chhako, deeper
hook: sharing as the shape of a life, not a donation

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam japo: remembrance underneath everything, like roots under a tree. Your line was the root. Did you catch a breath of remembering before any task? Today, the fruit. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

A boy is handed a bag of coins and sent to market. His father's instruction is simple: make a good deal, a true bargain, something that will turn a profit. On the road, the story says, the boy meets a group of holy men who have gone without food. He looks at the coins, and at them, and he buys food and feeds them. Then he walks home with an empty bag. His father is furious. The boy is Nanak, and the story gives his answer: that was the true bargain, sacha sauda, the true deal. Today, the third of the three phrases.
screen: `A BAG OF COINS.` → `HUNGRY MEN ON THE ROAD.` → `THE TRUE BARGAIN.`

segments.voice: Vand chhako. Vand means divide, share out. Chhako means eat, take your portion. Put them together and the order is the teaching: share, and eat. Not eat, and then, if there's anything left over, give some away. The sharing is built into the meal itself. That's the difference between a donation and a shape. A donation is something you do once in a while, on top of a life. A shape is the life. Guru Nanak's salok that we heard two days ago already holds it. The one who eats what he earns by his own effort, and gives something from his hand, that one recognizes the path. Earning and giving sit in the same sentence, the same breath. Giving isn't a separate department. And Sikh life made that shape visible. Tradition says Guru Nanak's community at Kartarpur farmed together and ate together, and it traces langar, the free kitchen, to that: a meal cooked and served to anyone who walks in, everyone sitting on the same floor, eating the same food. Nobody fills out a form to prove they're hungry. Nobody is asked their faith. That's vand chhako at the scale of a community. The Sacha Sauda story makes the same point in one afternoon. The father wanted a deal that turned a profit. The boy saw a deal that fed people, and called that the true one. So the deeper version of sharing isn't how much you give. It's whether giving comes first, before the asking, before the leftovers, before anyone has to explain themselves. That's today's line.
screen: `VAND: SHARE. CHHAKO: EAT.` · `A SHAPE, NOT A DONATION.` · `LANGAR: ONE FLOOR, ONE MEAL.` · `GIVING COMES BEFORE THE ASKING.` · then, large: `SHARE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share before you're asked. In the sit, breathe slowly, and let one person come to mind who could use something you have. Not necessarily money. Time, a meal, a ride, a skill, a phone call, attention. Notice whether they would ever ask. Some people never do. Choose the one thing you could offer without waiting for the request, and picture yourself offering it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each slow breath. The bell holds the time.
Vand chhako. Share, and eat: the sharing built into the meal and into the shape of a life, not added afterward. Today's word.
Your line: share first. Make the offer you chose in the sit before the day is out, before anyone has to ask. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice vand chhako through langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara where anyone may eat, through seva, and through dasvandh, setting aside a portion of what they earn to share.
